newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria says debt problems reduced.
newsitem.headline: Algeria says debt problems reduced.

text.p: Algerian Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia said on Saturday that Algeria had limited itself to borrowing slightly less than $2 billion in 1996, against a forecast of $3.8 billion.

Speaking to the Transitional National Council, Algeria's unelected quasi-parliament, Ouyahia gave no figure for the total foreign debt of the oil- and gas-producing country of 29 million people which officials have said is around $32 billion.

Algeria, which faced crippling debt servicing in 1994, rescheduled $5.109 billion of public debt in 1995 through the Paris Club. About $2 billion of private Algerian debt was rescheduled through the London Club in 1996.

Ouyahia, in his speech a copy of which was seen by Reuters, said Algeria, which is also trying to switch to a free-market economy after nearly three decades of state control, did not need another rescheduling.

He said according to forecasts drawn up at the time of the 1995 rescheduling, Algeria was to repay principal and interest totalling $6.658 billion in 1995, $5.787 billion in 1996, $4.468 billion in 1997, $3.599 billion in 1998, and $3.066 billion in 1999. He did not say if Algeria had stuck to the schedule in the past two years.
The prime minister said the debt-service ratio had fallen to around 32 percent in 1996 against a forecast 42.2 percent from 82.2 percent in 1993.
Foreign reserves stood at $4.230 billion at the end of 1996. Imports in 1996 totalled $10 billion against an expected $11 billion.
Non-energy exports for January-November had risen to $538 million, he said without giving a comparative figure.

With this increase and high prices for oil and gas which bring Algeria nearly 95 percent of its foreign income, the country had a trade surplus of $2.916 billion in the first 11 months of 1996 -- compared with a $1.209 billion deficit for the same period in 1995.
Ouyahia said the provisional current account balance for 1996 was a surplus of $150 million, against a forecast deficit of $2 billion.
He said the dinar, worth around 56 to the dollar at the end of 1996, had depreciated only seven percent during the year.
"Such a stabilisation of the exchange rate only two years after a heavy devaluation is not usual for countries which are in a phase of adjustment and (debt) rescheduling," he said.
But Ouyahia warned that despite the good performance, the government would pursue its austerity programme.

Servicing internal public debt totalling more than 2,000 billion dinars ($35.7 billion) drained 213.6 billion dinars from the treasury in 1996 and the figure wouldrise to 278.4 billion dinars in 1997.
For the first time, Algeria planned to make a repayment -- totalling 35.1 billion dinars -- of public internal debt.
It was also spending on modernising industry, much of which officials say operates at less than 50 percent capacity, with the aim of saving 400,000 jobs, Ouyahia said.

More would also be spent on housing. Lack of accommodation has been a running sore in Algiers and other cities and has fed the discontent which officials say drove many young people into the ranks of armed Moslem fundamentalists.
